Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Love 11:9: "Zehirut" [watchfulness] — the Torah uses this word in three senses. The first, in parashat Yitro, in the words of Yitro to Moses (Exodus 18:20), "and you shall warn [ve-hizharta] them of the statutes and the laws" — and our sages, of blessed memory, explained in Keritot, chapter "They said to him" (13b), on the verse (Leviticus 10:11), "and to teach the children of Israel all the statutes," etc. — that "statutes" refers to the homiletical expositions; we may expound similarly here that "statutes" refers to the homiletical expositions, and "the laws" refers to the Written Torah and the Oral Torah. And it says "ve-hizharta," showing that just as a warning is needed for negative commandments, so a warning is needed for positive commandments.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Love 11:10: The second sense is found in the Prophets, particularly many times in Ezekiel (Ezekiel 3:19), "and you, when you warn [hizharta] the wicked," etc. — and this is the essential warning regarding negative commandments, relevant to the exposition of the passage before us, "and you shall guard yourself from every evil thing, that a person should not have improper thoughts by day," etc., "from here Rabbi Pinchas said, zehirut" — thus zehirut is guarding [oneself].
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Love 11:11: Further, Scripture uses this word even for precise articulation of details, as David the king, peace be upon him, said (Psalms 19:11), "more desirable than gold... and sweeter than honey... indeed Your servant is careful [nizhar] with them" — and it is explained in the Idra of Ha'azinu (295b) that this is said of the letters gimel-yod-chaf-kof [the palatal letters], for the palate [chech] is mentioned in "his palate is sweetness" — and David the king, peace be upon him, was careful with these letters, to pronounce them properly in their articulation; and it says, in these words: gimel-yod-chaf-kof — "can that which is tasteless be eaten without salt" (Job 6:6), and it is written (Isaiah 32:17), "and the work of righteousness shall be peace" — "more desirable than gold and than much fine gold, and sweeter," etc. — "sweeter," indeed — David the king said, "indeed Your servant is careful with them" — I testify concerning myself that every day I am careful with them, not to err in them, except one single day. — end of quotation. From this we may derive that in all the precise articulations recorded in the words of our sages, of blessed memory, and in the books of the pious, one must be careful not to stumble in any of them.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Love 11:12: It follows that the word "zehirut" encompasses both the fulfillment of positive action and the observance of negative prohibitions, whether written in the Torah or in the words of the Sages — such as not gazing at a woman, even at her garments spread out on a wall, and many similar things. Perhaps because this word is all-encompassing, it is not counted among the ranked attributes in the Yerushalmi (Shabbat, ch. 1, halachah 3), which instead says: alacrity [zerizut] leads to cleanliness [nekiyut], cleanliness leads to purity [taharah], purity leads to holiness [kedushah]. Likewise, abstinence [perishut] is not counted among the attributes there, because abstinence and holiness are equivalent in their matter, as we shall explain, with God's help.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Love 11:13: "Zerizut" [alacrity] is a higher attribute than the preceding one, touching both positive and negative commandments — being watchful and swift in positive commandments, so that if a commandment comes into his hand, he performs it immediately, as it is said (Exodus 12:17), "and you shall guard the matzot [ha-matzot]" — and they expounded in the Mechilta (parashah 9): do not read "ha-matzot" but "ha-mitzvot" [the commandments] — just as one does not let matzah rise, so one should not let a commandment "rise" [be delayed] — rather, if the commandment comes into your hand, perform it immediately. — end of quotation. And likewise they expounded in the Mechilta on the verse (Joshua 3:1), "and Joshua rose early in the morning" — teaching that the alert rise early for commandments.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Love 11:14: The attribute of alacrity indicates the desire of one's soul and heart to perform that matter out of love of the Creator, and therefore he acts early rather than late, as the Tanna said (Avot 5:20) regarding the attribute of alacrity: be bold as a leopard, light as an eagle, swift as a deer, and mighty as a lion, to do the will of your Father in Heaven. When a person performs a matter with alacrity and joy, a new spirit and a spiritual spirit of life is added to him, such that he becomes light as an eagle; and this matter depends on removing from his heart the spirit of laziness and sadness, which is the external force that weighs down all of a person's limbs, such that he lacks the power to rise from his place either to study or to perform a commandment, as though all his limbs were dead. But if a person arouses his heart and removes that external force of laziness from himself by clinging to the desire of love of the Lord, who is the source of life, then his heart is alive, and he reads, studies, and performs his commandments with alacrity and joy to do the will of his Father in Heaven — and then strength is added to him, that he becomes light as an eagle, mighty as a lion, etc.; of this it is said (Isaiah 40:31), "but those who hope in the Lord shall renew their strength," etc., "they shall run and not grow weary, they shall walk and not faint."
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Love 11:15: The rule is that alacrity comes only through the desire of love, and therefore it is among the grades that lead to piety, which is love, as explained. Similarly, our sages, of blessed memory, explained in Bereishit Rabbah (55:8) on the verse (Genesis 22:3), "and Abraham rose early in the morning and saddled his donkey" — Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai said, love upsets the natural order — for did he not have servants? Rather, love upsets the natural order. — end of quotation, as pertains here.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Love 11:16: Without doubt, "and Abraham rose early in the morning" is alacrity, in the manner of "and Joshua rose early in the morning" as expounded, and it stems from love, and out of love he upset the natural order.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Love 11:17: In Sefer Beit Middot it is written regarding the attribute of alacrity, in these words: know, my children, that the rank of alacrity is an important attribute, for from the very beginning of man's creation he was created only to be alert in his deeds and his ways, as it is said (Genesis 2:7), "and man became a living soul [nefesh chayah]" — what is "chayah"? Alacrity — He made him a servant dependent on himself, so that if he does not toil he does not eat. See what is written regarding this (ibid. 2:15), "and He placed him in the Garden of Eden to work it and to guard it" — did it really need working and guarding? Rather, this was in order to spur him to alacrity. — end of quotation, as pertains here.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Love 11:18: Now, according to what our sages, of blessed memory, explained in Bereishit Rabbah, that "to work it and to guard it" refers to engaging in Torah and commandments, it follows that alacrity means to engage in Torah and commandments. They said in Bereishit Rabbah: "and He placed him in the Garden of Eden to work it and to guard it" — lest you say there is labor in the Garden of Eden, to dig and till the soil — do not all the trees grow of themselves? Or lest you say there is labor in the Garden of Eden to water the garden — does not a river flow out of Eden to water the garden? Rather, "to work it and to guard it" means to engage in words of Torah and to guard its commandments, as it is said (Genesis 3:24), "to guard the way to the tree of life," in the manner of (Proverbs 3:18), "it is a tree of life to those who hold fast to it." — end of quotation.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Love 11:19: In the Idra of Naso (141b), on the verse (Genesis 2:7), "and He breathed into his nostrils the breath of life, and man became a living soul" — it says: "and the Lord God formed the man" — who is male and female, "dust from the ground" — an image within an image, inward within inward, and all this why? In order to draw forth and to gaze, through it, into the concealment of the supernal concealed one, to the end of all concealments. This is what is written, "and He breathed into his nostrils the breath of life" — the breath of all life, above and below, depend on that soul and are sustained by it; "and man became a living soul" — to cling and to enter into rectifications in this manner, and to draw forth that soul from grade to grade until the end of all grades, so that that soul be found in all and spread throughout all, to be one alone; and whoever cuts this off from the world is as one who cuts off this very soul, and it appears as though there is another soul besides this one — and therefore he and his memory shall be cut off for all generations.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Love 11:20: Here is stated that the matter of "living soul" is said above, in Atzilut, regarding the secret of the supernal life that spreads from the Cause over all to all existing things, which is the breath of life for all the worlds; and by this reality, man below has within him a breath of life, and when he clings to his God in the secret of the supernal life, alacrity and a new spirit are given to him, and his heart and limbs come alive to do the will of his Maker, as explained above.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Love 11:21: Now, one who clings to the attribute of alacrity is clinging to the "woman of valor," a God-fearing woman [Malchut/Shechinah], in whom is the essence of all alacrity, as Solomon, peace be upon him, mentioned in her praises (Proverbs 31:15), "she rises while it is still night and gives food to her household," etc., "she girds her loins with strength and makes her arms firm," "she makes linen and sells it," "she watches over the ways of her household, and does not eat the bread of idleness." Here it is explicitly stated that all her attributes are performed with alacrity, and there is no bread of idleness in her, for the bread of idleness is in externality — "this also God has made corresponding to the other" (Ecclesiastes 7:14).
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Love 11:22: The reason further is that performing a commandment with alacrity indicates that one performs it with joy, and it is written (Psalms 100:2), "serve the Lord with gladness" — and it is known what our sages, of blessed memory, explained (Shabbat 30b), that the Shechinah rests only through joy, not through sadness or frivolity. It follows that through performing a matter with alacrity and joy, the Shechinah rests upon him; and one who performs it through laziness and sadness is punished, as it is written (Deuteronomy 28:47), "because you did not serve the Lord... with joy."
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Love 11:23: The explanation of "she does not eat the bread of idleness": "bread" refers to the food of a commandment or the Torah brought near to her, for the commandments are called "delicacies," as explained in the Tikkunim (Tikkunei Zohar Chadash 51a), "and make me delicacies as I love" (Genesis 27:4) — from the positive precepts; and likewise of the Torah it is said (Proverbs 9:5), "come, eat of my bread" — and when a person performs them with laziness, she [the Shechinah] does not eat them as she should, for of her it is said (Deuteronomy 4:24), "for the Lord your God is a consuming fire," and her eating is the Torah and commandments, as explained above; and since she does not eat them, they are cast outward.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Love 11:24: Therefore one must very much cling to alacrity and not to laziness, and of alacrity it is said (Proverbs 22:29), "you see a man diligent in his work" — namely, diligent in the work of the Shechinah, in whom is work, as explained in the Tikkunim (14b), and her "work," that is, her rectification, is the performing of Torah and commandments; and whoever holds fast to her with alacrity "shall stand before kings" — for ten kings are included in her, as explained in the Tikkunim — and "shall not stand before obscure ones" — the kelipot, which are darkness and not light. From the affirmative you understand the negative — that whoever, Heaven forbid, holds fast through laziness, clings to the obscure ones, and separates himself from the supernal holy angels.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Love 11:25: It says "shall stand [yityatzev]," and not "shall sit," for standing [yetziva] is upright, and it is known that all standing in the world represents the male (Zohar, parashat Tetzaveh 183a) — and the matter is that through his grasp of the Shechinah in the secret of the female waters through alacrity in the commandments, as explained, he ascends through her to the male world.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Love 11:26: It is also possible to say "yityatzev" in the manner our sages, of blessed memory, explained in the Mechilta on the verse (Exodus 14:13), "stand firm [hityatzevu] and see the salvation of the Lord," and likewise on the verse (Exodus 15:20), "and Miriam the prophetess took" — that "standing" everywhere refers to the holy spirit, in these words: "stand firm and see" — Israel said to him, when? He said to them, today the Shechinah rested upon you, the holy spirit — for "standing" everywhere refers only to the holy spirit, as it is said (Amos 9:1), "I saw the Lord standing over the altar, and He said, strike the capital," and it says (I Samuel 3:10), "and the Lord came and stood and called as at other times, Samuel, Samuel," and it says (Deuteronomy 31:14), "call Joshua and stand [hityatzevu] at the Tent of Meeting," and it says (Exodus 2:4), "and his sister stood [vatetatzav] at a distance" — and the holy spirit rested upon her. — end of quotation.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Love 11:27: On the verse "and Miriam the prophetess took," they explained that the verse "and his sister stood at a distance" is more compelling than all the others, for "at a distance," "to know what would be done" — all of this indicates the holy spirit.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Love 11:28: In the Zohar (parashat Acharei Mot, beginning of p. 301), they explained that Malchut is called "the holy spirit" when she nurses from the secret of Chochmah, being the spirit that nurses from the supernal sanctuary, which is Chochmah; therefore the word "standing" is fitting for her regarding the holy spirit. It follows from this that alacrity is a grade that leads to the holy spirit.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Love 11:29: It may also be said in another manner — we find it explained in Ra'aya Meheimna (parashat Kedoshim 82a) that Tiferet too possesses alacrity, in that it acts immediately from Abba and Imma without delay, in these words: and Israel, who are called "sons" — including "son" and "daughter" from the side of Tiferet and Malchut, who are son and daughter — [it is] the honor of their father and mother to perform His command, and His command is the positive precepts; and the masters of the Mishnah have already established, "there is one who is commanded and performs," and therefore he says "we shall do and we shall hear" — and this is the honor of Abba and Imma, that they command their son to act thus and he acts immediately without any delay at all. — end of quotation. In this manner it is explained in Chochmah too, and we quoted it in the Gate of Fear, end of chapter 2.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Love 11:30: In the Tikkunim, Tikkun 39 (79b), it is explained that Tiferet and Yesod, each, are called "commanded and performing" in the commandments included within the Shechinah, and accordingly, the alert person holds fast to the grade of the male world, and therefore "shall stand before kings," as explained.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Love 11:31: In any case, the essence of alacrity is in the place of action [Malchut], and depends upon her, for she serves the whole of Atzilut; and because of this, when the princes were lazy in the donation for the Tabernacle, the yod was lacking from them, which is the Shechinah, as it is said (Exodus 36:27), "veha-nesi'am hevi'u" ["and the princes brought"] — written "ha-nesi'am" deficient in the yod — and the reason, as explained, is that "she does not eat the bread of idleness." And I heard from the mouth of my master, may his rest be in Eden, that to rectify this, they brought at the dedication offering of the princes ten items — one silver bowl, one basin, etc. — you will find ten items there — and it is written "ha-nesi'im" fully spelled with a yod, [showing] that they hastened to bring this, in place of the laziness by which they had damaged the Shechinah.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Love 11:32: Know further, that alacrity is acquired in a person's soul only through fear, for one who fears the king is alert to perform his command and fears lest afterward some error be found in him; therefore he hastens to perform Torah and commandments. And likewise, for this reason alacrity applies correctly to the Shechinah, for there is [the attribute of] fear; and likewise cleanliness and purity are also branches of fear, for one must fear lest his garments be soiled before the King, but rather clean and pure — and likewise one must cleanse and purify his limbs and soul, since he stands always before the King of Kings, the Holy One, blessed and exalted be He.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Love 11:33: Further, regarding the attribute of alacrity, I found written in a manuscript book several particulars, which I saw fit to quote.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Love 11:34: "Nekiyut" [cleanliness] is used in four senses. The first, cleanliness and purification from sin and transgression, as it says (Numbers 5:31), "and the man shall be clean [ve-nikkah] from iniquity," and "and I shall be cleansed [ve-nikkeiti] from great transgression" (Psalms 19:14).
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Love 11:35: This attribute is needed for piety, which is love, for it is impossible, so long as there is a blemish on the soul, for love to cling to it. This is like the parable of a garment upon which oil or some other stain has fallen, that it cannot accept any dye until it is washed and that stain removed from it — so too, when the soul is soiled with the stains of its sins, if it is not cleansed and washed through repentance, and a particular repentance for each and every sin, as will be explained, it will not cling continuously to the supernal spirituality — for the sin is a partition separating him from his God, and therefore foreign thoughts will confuse him as he stands engaged in Torah or prayer.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Love 11:36: In the Yerushalmi, they brought proof that alacrity leads to cleanliness, as it is written (Leviticus 16:20), "and he shall finish [ve-chilah] atoning" — the matter being that "ve-chilah" indicates alacrity, since its meaning is the completion of the matter; and because the word "ve-chilah" seems superfluous there, in parashat Acharei Mot, regarding the service of Yom Kippur — for what need was there to say "ve-chilah," let it simply say "and he shall atone"? Rather, the intent surely is to indicate alacrity. And it says "mikaper" — the word "kapparah" [atonement] is explained as a term for wiping clean [purification], and this is an Aramaic word. And so Rashi, peace be upon him, explained in Tractate Chullin (8b), regarding the knife with which one slaughtered a treifah animal, where it says there, and if there is an old rag to wipe [le-mikhparei] it, it is not necessary [to discard the knife] — Rashi explained "balita" as a worn piece, "de-farsa," as we translate "the screen of the entrance" as "parsa"; "le-mikhparei" — to wipe it. And its counterpart in Gittin regarding Nevuzaradan, who wished "le-khapurei yadei" with that man [i.e., to cleanse his hands]; and in the Temple courtyard, the sprinkling basins are called "kefurei zahav" [golden basins], because one wipes his finger of blood [with them]. — end of quotation.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Love 11:37: Now, the word "kapparah" means purification and the wiping of a stain from a garment, so that no soiling at all remains upon it; and likewise, regarding the purification of sin, expressed in the language of "cleanliness," the meaning of "kapparah" is the concealment of that stain, the sin, from the soul. But when purification of sin is expressed in the language of "taharah" [purity], as it says (Psalms 51:4), "and purify me [taharani] from my sin" — "taharah" is the fine whitening of the garment, and this is what Rashi, of blessed memory, explained: "tahor" — bright, refined, superior to "clean." And likewise our sages, of blessed memory, also explained (Berachot 15a) regarding "I wash my hands in cleanliness [nikayon]" (Psalms 26:6), as "with anything that cleans," but purification is with water that purifies and refines things well.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Love 11:38: The reason that purity is needed after cleanliness may be understood from what Scripture says (Leviticus 13:58), "and the garment, or the warp, or the woof, or any vessel of skin, which you shall wash, and the plague has departed from it — it shall be washed a second time, and it shall be pure" — and this second washing is to impart to it a spirituality of holiness and purity, for when the plague departs from it, it remains without impurity, yet also without purity; and to impart to it a spirituality of purity, a second washing is needed.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Love 11:39: Further, it may be said, regarding the reason for the second washing, that although the plague has already departed — for the plague is one of the powers of Lilith, from whose side come the four appearances of plagues, as explained in the Tikkunim — when she attaches herself to a person or to his other vessels, she is attached in such a way that she does not depart quickly, but a trace of the impurity remains there, even though it is not visible to the eye, and that place where the plague was still bears a recognizable mark that she rested there; therefore, "it shall be washed a second time."
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Love 11:40: This is an extra advantage of holiness over impurity — for holiness, wherever it rests, never departs from there, as our sages, of blessed memory, explained (Megillah, ch. 3, mishnah 3) regarding a synagogue that has fallen into ruin, that one does not eulogize within it, etc., as it is said (Leviticus 26:31), "and I will make your sanctuaries desolate" — in their holiness they remain, even when desolate. But regarding impurity, although it is spiritual, with a second washing it is purified and refined, and that kelipah is utterly nullified.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Love 11:41: Likewise regarding repentance: even though a person has abandoned the sin completely and regretted it and never returned at all to his former deed, and purified himself through mortification, this does not suffice unless the accuser recognizes no trace of it in him at all, as though there had never been any sin in him at all — but rather, "it shall be washed a second time and it shall be pure," as though he had never sinned at all. This is what they said in the Yerushalmi, that cleanliness leads to purity, as it is said (Leviticus 12:8), "and the priest shall atone for her, and she shall be pure" — and what need is there for purity after atonement? Rather, because atonement is cleanliness and not essential purity, purity is additionally needed.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Love 11:42: We further find a second sense of "nekiyut," in what Scripture says regarding Avimelech (Genesis 20:5), "in the innocence of my heart and the cleanliness of my hands," and likewise (Psalms 24:4), "clean hands and a pure heart" — that one must strive to purify his hands from every serious matter and from anything that damages by means of the hands, as will be explained, with God's help.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Love 11:43: Some of these are explained in the Zohar (parashat Vayera 100b), in the interpretation of the verse "clean of hands," etc., in these words: come and see, "who shall ascend the mountain of the Lord" — and afterward it returns and explains "clean of hands" — one who does not use his hands for improper acts, nor does he act forcefully with them where it is unnecessary, and moreover does not defile himself with them nor defile his body with them, like those who defile themselves with their hands to become impure — this is "clean of hands."
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Love 11:44: The third [sense], what is said regarding the children of Gad and the children of Reuben (Numbers 32:22), "and you shall be clear [nekiyim] before the Lord and before Israel" — and our sages, of blessed memory, learned from here that a person must distance himself from suspicion, as we learn (Shekalim 3:2): the one collecting the terumah [chamber donations] enters neither with a hemmed cloak nor with shoes nor with sandals, lest he become poor and people say he became poor from the chamber's fund, or lest he become rich and people say he became rich from the chamber's terumah — for a person must be found innocent in the eyes of people just as he must be found innocent before the Omnipresent, as it is said, "and you shall be clear before the Lord and before Israel," and it says (Proverbs 3:4), "and find favor and good understanding in the eyes of God and man." Similar to this is what our sages, of blessed memory, said (Chullin 44b): distance yourself from ugliness and from that which resembles it.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Love 11:45: Further, a fourth interpretation is found, in the verse (Job 4:7), "remember now, who ever perished being innocent [naki]?" — and it is explained in the Zohar (parashat Pinchas 215b) that this refers to Pinchas, who was zealous for the covenant and did not defile it through the sin of Baal Peor with the daughters of Moab. It follows from this that "naki" is the attribute of the Righteous One [Tzaddik/Yesod], and therefore Pinchas was given the covenant of peace, as it is said (Numbers 25:12), "therefore, behold, I give him My covenant of peace." And so we find these two words together (Exodus 23:7), "and the innocent and the righteous you shall not slay" — showing that both are one matter. Regarding the "nekiyut" mentioned in the passage, the intent is that he be clean from anything that damages the sign of the covenant, which is in the Righteous One, so that he may be called "naki," which is in this same attribute.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Love 11:46: "Nekiyut leads to taharah" — although "taharah" has already been explained under the word "nekiyut," nevertheless there remains still to explain it, in the manner we expounded the preceding words: "taharah" is found in Torah, Prophets, and Writings in many senses; but what pertains to the matter of practical action are these: first, purity through immersion in forty se'ah [of water], as found many times in the Torah, among them (Leviticus 22:4), "any man of the seed of Aaron," etc., "shall not eat until he is pure"; and similarly, "and shall be unclean until evening, and then shall be pure," etc. (Leviticus 11:32), "and he shall bathe his flesh in living water and be pure" (Leviticus 15:13) — this is said regarding a zav, for whom the Torah required living water.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Love 11:47: Purity through immersion is a great aid for a person's soul to cling to his God and His service — for while he is impure, the impurity numbs a person's heart, as our sages, of blessed memory, explained above regarding "and you shall become impure through them" (Leviticus 11:43).
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Love 11:48: The essence of love and clinging depends on purity of heart from foreign thoughts, as David the king, peace be upon him, said (Psalms 51:12), "a pure heart God has created for me" — and so Rabbeinu Tam, peace be upon him, wrote in Sefer HaYashar (ch. 13), that purity of body renews purity in the soul. And while the body is impure, some blemish surely reaches the soul, and it is impossible for one to direct his intention properly without some other thought confusing him and separating him from the supernal root — for he is separated through the blemish upon his soul, as explained in the Tikkunim (52b), that He does not rest upon a blemished soul, as it is written (Leviticus 21:18), "anyone who has a blemish shall not approach." Therefore it is impossible for him to have clinging, for the essence of clinging is with the Cause of causes, the soul of all souls; and since He, exalted be He, does not rest upon him, how could he possibly cling to Him?
